hero.filename: Roman Bridge over the Esk at Musselburgh.jpg
hero.title: File:Roman Bridge over the Esk at Musselburgh.jpg
hero.source: Roman Bridge over the Esk at Musselburgh
hero.description: The Auld Brig dates from the 16th century, but is known locally as the 'Roman Bridge', because the Romans are known to have bridged the Esk at this spot. Many an English and Scottish army has crossed the bridge in its time. After the Battle of Pinkie in 1547, the routed Scottish army came under fire on the bridge from English ships at the mouth of the Esk and in 1745 Bonnie Prince Charlie's Jacobites crossed it on their way to and from the Battle of Prestonpans. This is the view looking northwards towards the river mouth.

gallery.title: File:Somerset's Mound, Inveresk Kirkyard.jpg
gallery.description:
An earthwork thrown up by the English forces during the Battle of Pinkie Cleugh. An information board at the entrance to the church explains that,
"The strategic position of this spot which attracted the Votadini tribe and the Romans also attracted the Duke of Somerset who formed a mound for his cannon in 1547. The former church was witness to the defeat of the 30,000 Scots army at the hands of the English when 10,000 Scots died. In 1650 Cromwell was similarly drawn to this site when he stabled his horses in the church. He placed cannon on Somerset's mound and built another behind the church which later disappeared to make room for burial plots."

gallery.filename: Protector Somerset marker stone at Pinkie, Musselburgh.JPG
gallery.title: File:Protector Somerset marker stone at Pinkie, Musselburgh.JPG
gallery.source: Protector Somerset marker stone at Pinkie, Musselburgh
gallery.description: This stone marks the site of the English army encampment on the eve of the battle of Pinkie in 1547. Edward Seymour, bearing the title Protector Somerset, led an English army with naval support into Scotland in a further attempt to force the Regent Arran and the Scottish nobility to agree to the marriage of the four-year old Mary, Queen of Scots, to the nine-year old King Edward VI of England. The battle turned into a disastrous defeat for the Scots, but the English did not press home the victory. In the following summer the Scottish Parliament agreed that the infant Queen should sail for France to marry the French Dauphin instead.
